title: The World of Concurrency
description: Understand what happens when multiple threads share resources — from race conditions and mutexes to deadlocks, async/await, and thread pools.

segments.text: Concurrency is where simple programs become tricky programs. The moment two threads share a variable, you enter a world where timing determines correctness. Let's learn to navigate it together.

First, a crucial distinction. Concurrency means dealing with multiple tasks — interleaving work on them. Parallelism means doing multiple tasks simultaneously. A single-core CPU can be concurrent but not parallel. It's like a juggler with one hand versus two.

Imagine two threads both reading a bank balance of one hundred dollars, then each adding fifty. They both write back one hundred fifty. But the correct answer should be two hundred! This is a race condition — the outcome depends on who runs first.

The fix? A mutex — mutual exclusion. It's a lock. Before touching shared data, a thread must acquire the lock. If another thread already holds it, you wait. Like a bathroom door lock — only one person at a time.
Mutexes solve race conditions, but they introduce a new problem. If every thread must wait for the lock, you've turned parallel work into serial work. The lock becomes a bottleneck.
segments.thought_prompt: If one mutex creates a bottleneck, what if we used two mutexes for different resources?

segments.text: Two mutexes can lead to something worse: deadlock. Picture the Dining Philosophers. Five philosophers sit at a round table, each needing two forks to eat. If every philosopher picks up the left fork and waits for the right fork — nobody eats. Ever.

In code, deadlock happens when Thread A holds Lock 1 and waits for Lock 2, while Thread B holds Lock 2 and waits for Lock 1. They're stuck forever, each waiting for the other. Your application freezes silently — no error, no crash, just nothing.

Now let's shift gears. Async/await is a different approach to concurrency. Instead of blocking a thread while waiting for I/O, the function suspends itself and says 'wake me when the data arrives.' The thread is free to do other work.

Thread pools are the pragmatic middle ground. Instead of creating and destroying threads constantly, you maintain a fixed pool of worker threads. Tasks go into a queue, and idle workers pick them up. Like having a fixed team of employees handling a stream of customer orders.

Choosing the right pool size is an art. Too few threads and you waste CPU on I/O waits. Too many and you waste memory and time on context switching. For CPU-bound work, match the core count. For I/O-bound work, you can go higher.
segments.thought_prompt: A web server mostly waits on database queries. Would you size its thread pool to the CPU core count or higher?

segments.text: Concurrency is powerful but demands respect. Race conditions corrupt data, mutexes serialize access, deadlocks halt progress, async/await avoids blocking, and thread pools manage resources. Master these patterns and you'll write systems that are both fast and correct.
